name: A Simple Problem
description: For an array $$$b$$$ of length $$$m$$$, define $$$f(b)$$$ as follows: An array $$$c$$$ of length $$$m$$$ is considered beautiful if and only if for each $$$1 \le i \le m$$$, $$$c_i$$$ either equals $$$\max(b_1,b_2,\ldots,b_i)$$$ or $$$\min(b_1,b_2,\ldots,b_i)$$$. Then, $$$f(b)$$$ is defined as the maximum number of inversions$$$^{\text{∗}}$$$ over all beautiful arrays. You are given a permutation$$$^{\text{†}}$$$ $$$p$$$ of length $$$n$$$. You need to answer $$$q$$$ queries, where each query contains two integers $$$l$$$ and $$$r$$$ ($$$1 \le l \le r \le n$$$). For each query, please compute $$$f([p_l,p_{l+1},\ldots,p_{r}])$$$. $$$^{\text{∗}}$$$The number of inversions of an array $$$a$$$ of length $$$n$$$ is defined as the number of pairs of integers $$$(i,j)$$$ such that $$$1 \le i \lt j \le n$$$ and $$$a_i \gt a_j$$$. $$$^{\text{†}}$$$A permutation of length $$$n$$$ is an array consisting of $$$n$$$ distinct integers from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$ in arbitrary order. For example, $$$[2,3,1,5,4]$$$ is a permutation, but $$$[1,2,2]$$$ is not a permutation ($$$2$$$ appears twice in the array), and $$$[1,3,4]$$$ is also not a permutation ($$$n=3$$$ but there is $$$4$$$ in the array).
input_specification: Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 10^4$$$). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$q$$$ ($$$1 \le n,q \le 10^6$$$), representing the length of $$$p$$$ and the number of queries, respectively. The second line contains $$$n$$$ distinct integers $$$p_1,p_2,\ldots,p_n$$$ ($$$1 \le p_i \le n$$$), representing the permutation $$$p$$$. Each of the next $$$q$$$ lines contains two integers $$$l$$$ and $$$r$$$ ($$$1 \le l \le r \le n$$$), representing a query. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ and the sum of $$$q$$$ over all test cases both do not exceed $$$10^6$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, output $$$q$$$ integers, where the $$$i$$$-th integer represents the answer to the $$$i$$$-th query.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 2210F — A Simple Problem [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
